topics.answer:
I'm Wrench, the assistant built into RobotForge. I am not a live AI and I don't call any model — every answer I give is assembled from RobotForge's recorded data in this repository: the Robodex (catalog/robots.json), the parts catalogue (catalog/parts.json) and the recorded gate reports (catalog/gate-reports.json).

If the data doesn't say it, I'll say so rather than guess.

Hello. I answer questions about RobotForge from its recorded data — the robots in the Robodex, their gate verdicts and measured numbers, the parts catalogue, and how the forge works.

Try one of the suggested questions, or ask about a robot by name.

The gate's thresholds are locked — printed on every report and never quietly loosened.

Distance error: pass ≤ 5%, marginal 5–10%, fail over 10%.
Heading error: pass ≤ 5°, marginal 5–10°, fail over 10°.

A run's verdict is set by its worst graded check.
samples: How much error is allowed before a robot fails?

topics.answer:
A gate run commands the robot's simulated twin to drive 1 metre and turn 90 degrees in Gazebo Sim.

The drive and turn are graded against the simulator's ground truth — where the robot actually went — and the robot's own odometry is graded against that same truth. A robot whose sensors are wrong about its own motion can't pass. When a check misses, the report names a suspect: the spec field to look at first.

link.label: See how the recorded runs were graded

topics.answer:
Marginal is the middle verdict: the measured error landed between the pass and fail bands — over 5% (or 5°) but not over 10% (or 10°).

It means 'close, but not inside the locked pass threshold'. A run's overall verdict is set by its worst check, so one marginal check makes the run marginal.

topics.answer:
RobotForge takes a robot from an idea to a measured verdict in five steps:

1. Input — describe the robot in plain words, show a photo, or paste a parts list.
2. Spec — Muse Spark drafts a structured spec: motors, wheels, battery, sensors, dimensions.
3. Checks — engineering validation catches numbers that don't add up, before anything is simulated.
4. Twin & gate — the spec becomes a digital twin that runs headless in Gazebo Sim, and the motion gate grades it against ground truth at locked thresholds.
5. Outputs — a URDF, a take-apart 3D-printable parts kit, and the gate's measured verdict.

This static site replays recorded runs — nothing here calls a model or a simulator live.

link.label: Step through a recorded run in the Forge

topics.answer:
In the Forge, pick the Words tab and write one paragraph about your robot: what it is, how it moves, roughly how big it is, what powers it and what sensors it carries.

Muse Spark turns the paragraph into a structured spec; the checks then grade the numbers, the twin is built, and the gate measures it. The Forge page replays a real recorded run of exactly this, step by step.
samples: How do I describe a robot?
How to describe a robot in words?

topics.answer:
Yes — a photo works as input. `robotforge describe --photo` has Muse Spark identify the robot and draft a spec from what is visible, and SAM cross-checks the visible part counts.

Honesty rule: a photograph carries no scale, so every dimension in a photo draft is ESTIMATED and labelled as such. The TurtleBot3 Waffle Pi in the Robodex arrived exactly this way — its spec is a photo draft and it has not been gated.
samples: Can I use a photo of a robot?

topics.answer:
A digital twin is the robot rebuilt in simulation from its spec: same dimensions, wheel layout and drive geometry, running headless in Gazebo Sim.

RobotForge grades the twin, not the physical robot — the gate measures whether the spec's model does what the spec claims. That distinction is printed wherever a verdict appears.

Every spec can become a take-apart kit (`robotforge cad`): one OpenSCAD file per part — chassis plate, wheels, motor mounts, brackets — plus an assembly and a parts index, sized from the spec's numbers and written for beginners to edit and 3D-print.

Each robot page in the app has a take-apart viewer that lays its kit out from the spec; click any part to see what it is.

link.label: Browse the robots and their kits

topics.answer:
Yes — paste a shopping or wish list into the Forge's Parts list tab (or run `robotforge import-list` in the repo): RobotForge identifies the parts against its catalogue, assembles a draft robot, suggests wiring, and lists what is missing.

The Forge replays a recorded import of a quadcopter parts list.

What happens with a shopping list?

topics.answer:
`robotforge lookup` takes a robot the forge identified — from words or a photo — finds its official open-source model (for example a URDF in the maker's repository), and pulls it with its licence and a manifest, so real robots enter the Robodex with provenance attached.

The TurtleBot3 models in the Robodex arrived this way.

topics.answer:
The catalogue doesn't carry shop links or prices yet — each part's buy field is deliberately empty in this version. That's a planned later step, not something I can paper over.

What the catalogue does record for every part is its source and licence. Ask me about a part by name and I'll tell you what it is, what it's used for, and where the entry came from.
samples: Where can I buy the parts?
How much does a part cost?

topics.answer:
I answer from RobotForge's recorded data. Ask me:

• about a robot by name or Robodex number — 'Tell me about the Burger', 'Why did Andino fail?'
• which robots passed or failed the gate
• how the gate works and what its thresholds are
• about any part in the catalogue by name — 'What is a TB6612FNG?'
• how RobotForge works, or how to describe a robot

If the recorded data doesn't cover it, I'll say so plainly.
